cadence · 3

Candidate Law cadence
weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 41% of 34 measurements 17 channels
Find a stable upload cadence and keep it, so the channel becomes part of viewers' weekly patterns; consistency of rhythm matters, not just raw frequency.
Source: Mario Joos
Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Merged 1 duplicate (2026-09-01): The duplicate additionally asserted consistency matters MORE THAN the interval itself — a comparative no current probe tests. If a probe ever compares the two, that claim deserves re-opening as its own question. Decomposed into 2 atomic claims by our strategist (directed in chat 2026-09-02, executed by Claude) (2026-09-02).

Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: shipping on the channel's usual rhythm → first-28-day views vs off-rhythm uploads (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived on the channel's usual rhythm out-perform ones that broke it?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for uploads arriving within half the channel's typical 48.0-day gap, minus the same for uploads that broke the rhythm.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 60 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

What this does not tell you
  • The smallest group behind this is 4 videos. At that size a couple of unusual uploads can carry the whole result.

Measured refinement — Median days between uploads per channel (40 most recent uploads)

Measured directly: the median channel uploads every 11 days (middle half 7-21.1). The claim is about KEEPING a rhythm, not about its length; this shows what rhythms the fleet actually runs, which is the range any "weekly" advice has to survive.

Window: 83 channels with 8+ dated uploads; gaps over the 40 most recent. Each dot is one channel's median; hover a dot for its name.

ideation · 2

Candidate Law ideation · earlier check spanned 52 channels Contested
weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 31% of 39 measurements 18 channels
Making a subject the 'world's largest/fastest/most expensive' version of a thing is a design decision that manufactures uniqueness, because a superlative topic has no direct competition on YouTube by construction.
Source: Paddy Galloway
Contested — what would settle it

Does the depth of evidence (videos behind each side, effect sizes, risk asymmetry) justify acting on this where the count of channels does not?

Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Data rejection overridden by our strategist (2026-09-02): Directed in chat 2026-09-02 on the depth lens: the count basis rejects at 33% held, but the per-channel effect interval supports it (+0.34, 95% 0.02 to 0.67, k=18) and the risk is asymmetric — median |effect| 0.94 where it held against 0.09 where it failed. Large upside, negligible downside: worth acting on and keeping measured.

Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: making the subject a world-superlative version of a thing (surfaced via superlative titling) → first-28-day views (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: Do titles escalating to a superlative earn more views than plain ones?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for titles containing a superlative or scope claim minus the same for titles without one, scaled by the pooled median.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 46 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Brief: superlative delta -0.06 (maker-builds, n=21), -0.01 (motorcycle, n=48), -0.05 (roblox, n=51) — negative in all three niches. My corpus check across 46 channels: WITH n=21 median 1.01x vs 1.00x (p=0.71); age-adjusted 0.98x vs 1.00x (p=0.52); 1 of 3 channels with >=2 matches came out ahead. Our own channels: n=4, median 0.75x. The library agrees: 'The World's Most ___' 1.09x, "World's Most ___ People" 0.98x, 'I Made the World's Most <SUPERLATIVE> <THING>' 0.84x — three of the four lowest-lift formats we have mined. Channel G' 'I built "the world's best speakers"' returned 0.75x against his own median.

Caveat: Title keywords are an imperfect stand-in for a genuinely superlative SUBJECT — a video can be about the world's largest thing without saying so in the title. Sample sizes for the tight regex are small (n=21 corpus, n=4 ours) even though three independent measurements agree on direction. The claim's premise (no direct competition) is not itself tested; only its performance consequence is.

Disputed

The count basis rejects this (held in 31% of readings across 18 channels); our strategist overrode the rejection: Directed in chat 2026-09-02 on the depth lens: the count basis rejects at 33% held, but the per-channel effect interval supports it (+0.34, 95% 0.02 to 0.67, k=18) and the risk is asymmetric — median |effect| 0.94 where it held against 0.09 where it failed. Large upside, negligible downside: worth acting on and keeping measured.

Settle it by answering: Does the depth of evidence (videos behind each side, effect sizes, risk asymmetry) justify acting on this where the count of channels does not?

Where the claim came from
I talked about my latest Mark Rober video about how he does like the world's largest videos. So by design, that's unique because now it's the number one. There's no other competition.
Candidate Law ideation · Maker / build · earlier check spanned 37 channels
strong Reproduced The same relationship showed up on independent channels. Much harder to explain as coincidence — still not a demonstrated cause. held 75% of 28 measurements 8 channels
A near-duplicate of a proven format outperforms a wholly new one because familiarity does the work of removing risk while a small novel element supplies the reason to click — roughly a 90/10 split of template to twist.
Source: Alan Garnett
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

WHERE ON THE EXPOSURE CURVE is this format for this audience? Gannett already holds the reconciling pattern (115f4acc5069): liking follows an inverted-U against exposure count, rising with repetition to a peak and falling after, so a format has a finite number of uses. Both claims are true, on opposite sides of the peak — which converts an argument into a measurement problem: what is the instalment count, and is per-instalment performance still rising? Our mined-format table is weakly consistent with the decay side and worth watching rather than citing: the highest observed lifts sit on small match counts (I Built My Own After Getting Screwed, n=4, 2.92x; Exposing N Secrets, n=3, 2.76x) while the largest cohort in the table (Product Full Review, n=16) sits at 1.67x. That is confounded by naming granularity and cannot carry weight yet, but the store should record instalment index alongside every format so the peak becomes observable rather than argued about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Corpus (33 channels, 831 videos): near-duplicates median 0.980x vs unique 1.005x (MWU z=-1.68, p=0.093). Age-adjusted the gap widens against repetition: 0.954x vs 1.016x (n=278 vs 534, z=-2.67, p=0.0076). Only 15 of 33 channels had repeats beating uniques. Our channels on first-28d views: repeated 0.99x (n=18) vs unique 1.00x (n=101), p=0.95. Conditional test, strict format frames (signature carrying >=2 literal frame words): 9 pairs where the prior instance scored >=1.5x produced follow-ups with median 1.01x and 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x (base rate 7%); median ratio next/prev = 0.29. Our channels: 3 such pairs, next median 0.72x, ratio 0.45, 0 of 3 reaching 1.5x.

Caveat: Signature repetition is a proxy for 'near-duplicate of a proven format' and catches generic title habits as well as deliberate franchises; a creator could execute the 90/10 rule without the title showing it. The conditional test that isolates deliberate repeats-of-a-hit is the strongest evidence but rests on only 12 pairs. Regression to the mean guarantees some decline from a >=1.5x instance regardless of format logic — but the claim asserts near-duplicates beat wholly new videos, and they do not beat them even before conditioning on a prior hit.

Where the claim came from
With a meme, you already know 90% of the joke. In this case, you know that grumpy Cat is grumpy, Ohanian told me. What makes it funny is the 10% twist, or what the caption is.

The claim's own evidence ('longest curves were disproportionately high-view') is exactly the confounded within-channel version.

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived in a daily burst (within ~1.5 days of the previous upload) underperform the channel's non-burst baseline?

Exact arithmetic: Median age-normalised views for 10 uploads arriving within 1.5 days of the previous upload, minus the same for 221 non-burst uploads.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 21 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

Showing the 12 most recent of 46 readings.

Effect is signed toward the claim: a positive number means the claim's own prediction showed up, whichever way the raw statistic pointed. Figures are differences of medians, scaled by the pooled median.

Correlation. The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause.

What this does not tell you
  • The smallest group behind this is 3 videos. At that size a couple of unusual uploads can carry the whole result.
  • 26 readings from public-seeded channels (lifetime views, no analytics grant) are shown in the table but excluded from every figure here — swapping views bases flipped 1 in 5 verdicts when tested, so the two are not pooled.
  • It did NOT hold on Channel I, The Mountain Maker, Channel K, Josh Prime, Thrift Diving (Serena Appiah), Mercanthony, Channel B, Mission Side Hustle, monica razak, Thrilled Thrifter, Julie Thrifts, Mission Side Hustle, monica razak, Channel I, The Mountain Maker, Thrilled Thrifter, Thrift Diving (Serena Appiah), Julie Thrifts, Mercanthony, The Carpenters Daughter, Channel A, Channel B, Channel D, KARLY ALANE, ColeyDoesThings. Those channels are the interesting ones: whatever they do differently is the missing context.

A group needs 3 channels before it gets a figure. Fewer is not "untested there" — it is measured and under-sampled, so the row stays and the number does not. These splits never move a claim's standing; they only say who the evidence came from. 2 of the underlying stamps are backfill reconstructions — the channel's conditions as of the backfill date, not measurement time.
